summary: Lays out interworking requirements for running MPLS-TE as a client network over a GMPLS network, which can give better operations than separate management. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This lists what must work when one kind of traffic-engineered network sits on top of another one.

questions: how do mpls-te and gmpls interwork
subtitle: Operating traffic-engineered networks as clients of generalized networks.

tldr.problem: Internet providers operate MPLS traffic engineering networks on top of transport networks, and increasingly these transport networks use GMPLS control. The two protocols need to work together effectively.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines requirements for interworking between MPLS-TE (which controls packet networks) and GMPLS (which can control packet, optical, and other technologies). Border routers at the interface between the two networks must handle both protocols and coordinate their operations.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can build more efficient multi-layer networks where MPLS-TE networks automatically trigger setup of underlying GMPLS paths and maintain independence between the two layers.

today: This RFC describes a framework and requirements that have guided implementations of MPLS-TE over GMPLS networks in service provider environments. The Border Peer Model it recommends is commonly used in production networks. The RFC has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Two-Layer Problem
sections.content:
MPLS-TE (Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering) is a protocol for controlling how data packets are routed through a network to meet quality-of-service requirements. It was designed for packet-switching networks.

GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) is a newer framework that extends MPLS concepts to control not just packet networks, but also optical, time-division, and other layer-1 and layer-2 technologies. Service providers often run MPLS-TE networks as clients on top of GMPLS-controlled transport networks.

This document examines what needs to happen for these two systems to interwork smoothly. The challenge is that MPLS-TE assumes a packet network underneath, while GMPLS might control very different technologies.
sections.eli5: Two different traffic control systems need to work together even though they were designed for different types of networks.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
The RFC describes a layered architecture: MPLS-TE client networks sit on top of a GMPLS server network. At the boundary between them are Border Routers that speak both protocols.

An end-to-end MPLS-TE path originates and terminates on Label Switched Routers (LSRs) in the client network. This path passes through the GMPLS server network, which provides transparent transport. The GMPLS network may be a single technology (like optical) or multi-layer (combining multiple technologies).

Inside each MPLS-TE client network, standard MPLS-TE routing and signaling work normally. Inside the GMPLS network, standard GMPLS protocols work normally. Border Routers translate between the two and manage the crossing of paths from one layer to the other.
sections.eli5: Border Routers act like translators: they speak the language of the upper network on one side and the lower network on the other.

sections.title: What Must Work
sections.content:
The RFC lists detailed requirements. First, end-to-end signaling must preserve MPLS control information across the GMPLS network. Second, triggered setup must allow GMPLS paths to be automatically created when MPLS-TE LSPs are requested, controlled by policy.

Third, diverse paths must be available to protect against failures in both layers. Fourth, TE information exchange must let MPLS routers compute paths that cross the GMPLS network. Fifth, selective advertisement must prevent incompatible information from the lower layer confusing the upper layer.

Sixth, protection interworking ensures that if MPLS-TE LSPs request fast reroute protection, the GMPLS network provides equivalent protection. Seventh, independent recovery allows each layer to handle failures without disrupting the other. Eighth, the solution must not introduce unnecessary complexity or risk.

Additional requirements cover scalability (in terms of network size and number of LSPs), performance (failure recovery and control-plane overhead), and management (diagnostics and coordination across layers).
sections.eli5: The upper network must be able to set up paths automatically, protect them if things break, and keep information from the lower network from causing confusion.

sections.title: Trust and Access Control
sections.content:
Border routers sit at administrative domain boundaries. Unlike typical inter-domain scenarios, the border router is fully part of both networks and participates in the security procedures of both.

The critical security concern is policy enforcement. The GMPLS server network (lower layer) must protect itself from disruptive behavior in the client networks. For example, clients might repeatedly request setup and teardown of LSPs, overloading the server network's control plane. Border routers must enforce policies to prevent this.

Equally important is access control for operators. Operators of the client MPLS-TE network must not be able to configure the server GMPLS network, and vice versa. However, a single operator may have privileges in both networks, and operators may need read-only access to status information across layers.

The RFC notes that authentication and access control mechanisms are not part of GMPLS protocols themselves; they depend on management plane implementations.
sections.eli5: Operators need clear permissions: you can run the top layer, you can run the bottom layer, and they both need to trust the border router in the middle.

sections.title: Recommended Approach
sections.content:
The RFC recommends the Border Peer Model. In this model, the Border Router participates fully as a peer in both the client and server networks, giving it complete visibility into both. However, it does not distribute routing information from one layer into the other.

This contrasts with the Overlay Model, where there is only a request-response interface and no shared routing information. The Border Peer Model is more efficient because Border Routers can make better decisions with full knowledge of both layers.

For the actual paths across the server network, the RFC recommends using hierarchical LSPs (where an entire server-layer path is treated as a single link by the client layer) over contiguous LSPs (which blend the two protocols). This approach allows more flexibility and easier independent failure recovery.

The RFC also discusses how MPLS-TE control plane messages can be carried through the GMPLS network and provides guidance on Fast Reroute protection in different scenarios.
sections.eli5: The best approach is to make Border Routers smart enough to coordinate everything, but keep the two layers' routing information separate so they don't confuse each other.
